checks.title: Password hash sync on
checks.remediation: Enable password hash synchronization in Entra Connect, even alongside pass-through authentication or federation, for leaked credential detection and sign-in failover.

userImpact.text: Password hashes sync in the background; users sign in as before.

checks.narrative: Without the hashes in Entra, leaked credential detection has nothing to compare and a federation outage is a sign-in outage.

checks.title: Hard and soft match takeover protection on
checks.remediation: Set BlockSoftMatch and BlockCloudObjectTakeoverThroughHardMatch on the directory synchronization features.

userImpact.text: A sync setting users never see.

checks.narrative: An on-premises account that matches a cloud admin by UPN or source anchor takes it over on the next sync. The two switches close that path.

checks.title: No federated domains, or a dated migration plan
remediation: Move each federated domain to password hash sync or pass-through authentication with staged rollout, recording the plan as an exception while it runs.
Decommission AD FS.

userImpact.text: Users sign in on the Microsoft page instead of the AD FS page, once the domain is converted.

checks.narrative: ADFS is a Tier 0 server farm whose only purpose Entra now performs natively. Every federated domain keeps it alive.

checks.title: Entra Connect Health with no open alerts
checks.remediation: Install the Connect Health agent on the sync server and work the open alerts.

userImpact.text: Monitoring users never see.

checks.narrative: Sync errors, an aging sync server and a stale export show up in Connect Health first, long before users notice.

checks.title: Domain Admins within the limit
checks.remediation: Reduce Domain Admins to five or fewer named, separate admin accounts; delegate everything else.

userImpact.text: People removed from Domain Admins use a delegated role for their tasks.

checks.narrative: Every Domain Admin is a path to every system. Service accounts and daily-use accounts in the group are the usual excess.

checks.title: Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins empty
checks.remediation: Empty both groups; add a member only for the forest change that needs it, then remove it.

userImpact.text: Nobody uses these groups day to day.

checks.narrative: Neither group has a day-to-day purpose. Standing members are standing forest-wide control.

checks.title: Operator groups empty or justified
checks.remediation: Remove members from Account, Server, Print and Backup Operators, DnsAdmins and Group Policy Creator Owners, or record each as an exception.

userImpact.text: People removed from operator groups use a delegated role for their tasks.

checks.narrative: These groups grant quiet paths to domain control: a Backup Operator can read the AD database, a DnsAdmin can load a DLL on a DC.

checks.title: Admin accounts hardened: Protected Users, no delegation, no SPN, no mailbox, fresh password
remediation: Put admin accounts in Protected Users.
Mark them sensitive and cannot be delegated.
Remove their SPNs and mailboxes.
Rotate passwords older than a year.

userImpact.text: Admin accounts lose cached sign-in on servers and must use Kerberos; some old tools may stop working for them.

checks.narrative: adminCount=1 marks the accounts AdminSDHolder protects. Each listed issue is a way an attacker turns one of them into domain control.

checks.title: krbtgt password rotated within the window
remediation: Rotate the krbtgt password with Microsoft's script.
Rotate it a second time at least ten hours later.
Schedule the rotation every six months.

userImpact.text: Rotated twice ten hours apart, users notice nothing.

checks.narrative: A krbtgt password from years ago means any golden ticket ever forged still works.

checks.title: Built-in Administrator and Guest controlled
checks.remediation: Disable the RID 500 account (keep its password in the break-glass safe) and the Guest account.

userImpact.text: Nobody signs in with these accounts.

checks.narrative: RID 500 cannot be locked out and is the first account any attacker tries.

checks.title: Machine account quota zero
checks.remediation: Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 on the domain and let the provisioning process join computers.

userImpact.text: Users can no longer join computers to the domain themselves; IT or Autopilot does it.

checks.narrative: The default lets any user create ten computer accounts, the first step of several Kerberos relay and delegation attacks.

checks.title: No unconstrained delegation outside domain controllers
checks.remediation: Remove unconstrained delegation from the listed objects; use constrained or resource-based delegation where a service needs it.

userImpact.text: A service that relied on unconstrained delegation may need constrained delegation configured.

checks.narrative: A server trusted for unconstrained delegation holds the tickets of everyone who connects to it, including Domain Admins.

checks.title: No Kerberoastable user accounts
checks.remediation: Move services to group managed service accounts; for the rest set long random passwords, AES only, and no privileged membership.

userImpact.text: Services moved to managed service accounts may need a restart; users notice nothing.

checks.narrative: Any domain user can request a ticket for an SPN and crack the password offline. A user account with an SPN and an old password is already lost.

checks.title: No AS-REP roastable accounts
checks.remediation: Re-enable Kerberos pre-authentication on the listed accounts.

userImpact.text: Users sign in as before.

checks.narrative: Without pre-authentication an attacker gets crackable material for the account without a password.

checks.title: Windows LAPS on member computers
checks.remediation: Deploy Windows LAPS through Intune or GPO to every workstation and member server, and retire legacy LAPS.

userImpact.text: The local admin password rotates in the background.

checks.narrative: Without LAPS the local administrator password is shared across the fleet and one workstation compromise is every workstation.

checks.title: Forest and domain functional level 2016 or higher
checks.remediation: Raise the functional levels once the last older domain controller is gone.

userImpact.text: Users notice nothing.

checks.narrative: Older levels keep older Kerberos and replication behaviours alive, and block Protected Users and the Recycle Bin features.

checks.title: Domain controllers on supported Windows Server, two or more
checks.remediation: Replace the listed domain controllers with Windows Server 2016 or later and keep at least two per domain.

userImpact.text: Done in a maintenance window, users notice nothing.

checks.narrative: An unsupported domain controller is an unpatched Tier 0 server. One domain controller is a single point of failure for every sign-in.

checks.title: AD Recycle Bin enabled
checks.remediation: Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin optional feature; it cannot be turned off again.

userImpact.text: Users notice nothing.

checks.narrative: Deleted objects come back with their attributes and group membership instead of from backup.

checks.title: No stale enabled users beyond the window
remediation: Disable enabled accounts that have not signed in within the stale window and move them to a quarantine OU.
Delete them after the retention period.

userImpact.text: Accounts nobody has used are disabled; their owners, if any, ask to be re-enabled.

checks.narrative: Stale enabled accounts are the leavers the process missed; each one is a valid credential nobody watches.

checks.title: Password policy: 14 characters, lockout on, no reversible encryption
remediation: Set the default domain policy to 14 characters or longer, with lockout.
Add a stricter fine-grained policy for admin and service accounts.

userImpact.text: Users set a longer password at their next change, and repeated wrong passwords lock the account for a while.

checks.narrative: The default domain policy is what every account without a fine-grained policy inherits.

checks.title: No people exempt from the domain's password expiry
remediation: Prefer ending scheduled expiry for everyone (HY-031) once MFA and Password Protection on-premises are in place; this check then passes with nothing else to change.
While the domain still expires passwords, clear Password never expires on the people listed and move service accounts to group managed service accounts.

userImpact.text: The people listed change their password on the domain's schedule, unless the domain stops expiring passwords for everyone.

checks.narrative: While the domain expires passwords, a person flagged Password never expires is an exception nobody reviews, often a shared login or a service account someone signs in with. NIST SP 800-63B favours ending scheduled expiry for everyone (HY-031); until then the exceptions should go.

checks.title: SID filtering on every external trust
checks.remediation: Enable SID filtering quarantine on the listed trusts, and selective authentication where the trust is external.

userImpact.text: Users of the trusted domain sign in as before, unless they relied on SID history.

checks.narrative: A trust without SID filtering lets the other forest inject your privileged SIDs into its tokens.

checks.title: Seamless SSO key rotated within the window
checks.remediation: Roll the AZUREADSSOACC Kerberos decryption key every 30 days with the Entra Connect PowerShell module.

userImpact.text: A key rotation users never see.

checks.narrative: The seamless SSO computer account's key signs Kerberos tickets for Entra; an old key is a long-lived forgery path.

checks.title: No AD CS templates open to ESC1
checks.remediation: On each listed template, remove Enrollee supplies subject or require manager approval, and restrict enrollment permissions.

userImpact.text: People who request certificates from the template may need approval.

checks.narrative: A published template that lets the requester name the subject and issues client authentication certificates lets any enrollee become any user, including a Domain Admin.

checks.title: No credentials in Group Policy
remediation: Remove the Group Policy Preferences that carry cpassword values.
Rotate the passwords they held.

userImpact.text: Users notice nothing; the old passwords stop working once rotated.

checks.narrative: The cpassword encryption key has been public since 2012; any domain user can read SYSVOL.

checks.title: Domain passwords do not expire on a schedule
remediation: Set Maximum password age to 0 (never) in the Default Domain Policy, once MFA and Entra Password Protection on-premises are in place (ID-019).
Keep a stricter fine-grained policy for service and admin accounts that need rotation by design, and rotate those with a vault.

userImpact.text: People stop being made to change their Windows password every few weeks.

checks.narrative: NIST SP 800-63B advises against periodic password changes; they produce predictable patterns and help desk calls. With a long minimum length, a banned list and MFA, a change belongs after a suspected compromise, not on a calendar.

checks.title: Groups that grant cloud access are managed in Entra, not in AD
remediation: Start with the groups left out of Conditional Access policies: switch their source of authority to Entra (Group Source of Authority, in the Entra admin center or through Graph), or replace them with groups created in Entra.
Where the group still grants access to something on-premises, provision it back to AD with Entra Cloud Sync group provisioning after the switch, so AD keeps a copy that only Entra changes.
Then do the same for the groups that assign licences, and keep new access groups cloud-native.

userImpact.text: Nothing changes for members: the group keeps its name and members; only who can edit it moves from AD to Entra.

checks.narrative: A group synced from Active Directory is changed in Active Directory. Anyone who can edit it there (a domain admin, an account operator, a delegated OU administrator, or an attacker who reached a domain controller) decides who a Conditional Access policy leaves out or who gets a licence and its apps, and the change reaches the cloud with the next sync. Switching the group's source of authority to Entra keeps the access decision with Entra administrators, and Cloud Sync can still write the group back to AD for on-premises apps.

checks.title: Groups synced from AD moved to Entra management
remediation: List the synced groups that only serve cloud apps, Teams, SharePoint or licences, and switch their source of authority to Entra a batch at a time.
For groups that also control on-premises access, switch them and turn on Cloud Sync group provisioning to AD so both sides stay in step.
Replace groups whose membership follows a rule (department, office, job title) with dynamic groups in Entra, and give group owners the members to manage in My Groups.

userImpact.text: Group owners manage members in My Groups or Teams instead of asking IT to change Active Directory, and changes apply at once instead of at the next sync; members notice nothing.

checks.narrative: Much of what Entra does for groups works only on groups it manages: dynamic membership, role-assignable groups, PIM for Groups, access reviews that remove people, access packages that add them, expiration and naming policies, and owners managing their own members. A group still managed in AD gets none of it, and every change waits for a sync. Microsoft now lets a synced group's source of authority move to Entra without recreating it, and users the same way (Connect Sync 2.5.76.0 or Cloud Sync 1.1.1370.0 and later).

checks.title: No open Defender for Identity health issue
remediation: Open each issue in the Defender portal, Settings, Identities, Health issues: it says which sensor or domain controller and what to do.
Fix the cause: start or reinstall the sensor, give the directory service account what it needs to read, or install a sensor on a domain controller that has none.
Close an issue that is fixed, and suppress only one that is understood and accepted.

userImpact.text: None for users. A sensor that is fixed starts watching its domain controller again.

checks.narrative: Defender for Identity sees an attack on Active Directory only through its sensors on the domain controllers. A sensor that has stopped, a domain controller with no sensor, or a service account that can no longer read leaves a blind spot exactly where lateral movement and credential theft happen, and nothing else in the tenant says so. Every issue Defender for Identity has open is listed, the most severe first.
